title: Scenes that leave something to notice
statement: Give a still scene meant for inference rich detail and meaningful activity beyond the foreground, leave its implications unexplained, and have students support an interpretation with what they noticed.
detail: Machine-made notes of a design meeting recorded a proposal for a world students could read for themselves: rich detail without explaining the implications, meaningful activity beyond the foreground, and asking what students notice and what it implies. Review found the comic intro prototype had reduced this to a presentation style, and that narration explaining every detail while the pictures repeat it misses the point. The build direction was then reset to rich scenes worth examining and space for students to think, and the reset was endorsed.
against: 'These are transcript attributions from the generated notes, not independently verified audio.' (`g9/transcript/chat-transcript.redacted.txt`, line 6017). Not tried with students. In a film that explains, eye-catching motion behind the explanation is barred, so this holds for still scenes meant for noticing.

evidence.quote: you were proposing a world students could read for themselves. I had reduced that too much to a presentation style.
Give the situation rich detail, “without explaining the implications” (p.10).
Put meaningful activity beyond the foreground: your example was Othello and Desdemona with people plotting behind them (pp.15–16).

If the narration explains the significance of every detail and the pictures merely repeat it, it still misses your point. We should provide the context, let the student inspect the scene, then ask them to support an interpretation with what they noticed.
a mature illustrated-book experience, rich scenes worth examining, compelling narration, quiet optional help, and space for students to think.
